What official or repeated statements from promoters, bookers, or creative teams reveal the company’s guiding principles on match finishes, long-term storytelling vs. short-term wins, and when to prioritize spectacle over competitive legitimacy?
sub_answers.text:
Creative decisions on match finishes and long-term storytelling have been made by bookers and booking committees rather than by in-ring competition, with titles awarded by scripted match endings chosen by bookers [d53518967s0p0] [d22220471s0p0].
Promoters and committees have created formal rules and structures to guide show presentation and champion recognition, such as the Admiral-Lord Mountevans rules that established weight divisions and formal championship crowns [d697832s3p0].
When injuries or sudden changes occurred, booking committees altered plans and outcomes for major events, weighing short-term fixes against longer-term storytelling (for example, changing title plans for Souled Out after champion injuries) [d584966s4p0].
Promoters have prioritized spectacle in on-screen presentation by scripting authority-figure storylines and faction-based spectacles to modernize company direction and entertainment value [d584966s4p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: In concrete terms, how have stables or factions been used on event cards—e.g., multi-man title shots, elimination tags, faction vs. faction specials—and what rules or contract stipulations govern faction members’ access to singles titles and tournament seeding?

Factions have been used as large, named groupings for storyline conflict, exemplified by the on-screen faction war "The New Blood vs. The Millionaire's Club" [d584966s4p0].
Tag-team championships were promoted regionally and used to highlight team-based competition within territories, indicating regular inclusion of multi-person teams on cards [d53518967s0p0].

Which named recurring shows, cups, round-robin leagues, or single-elimination tournaments has the company run specifically to select number-one contenders or establish faction dominance, and what were the formats and reward structures for each?
sub_answers.text:
Promoters sometimes announced champions as tournament winners even when no tournament records exist, as when the Sharpe brothers were promoted as having won a tournament upon arrival in Indianapolis [d53518967s0p0].
Major pay-per-view events such as Souled Out have been used to implement revised title plans and special-match concepts, including rumble-style matches considered to deliver sudden title changes [d584966s4p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: When wrestlers were suddenly injured, released, or left for other promotions, what documented booking steps did creative teams take (vacating titles, interim champions, storyline injury angles, postponed main events), with examples and timeline of how matches/feuds were rewritten?
sub_answers.text:
When Bret Hart and Jeff Jarrett reported injuries and could not wrestle, creative teams were required to vacate their championships and sit down to rework plans for the Souled Out event [d584966s4p0].
Bookers proposed alternate finishes and potential short-term champions (for example the plan to put a vacated WCW Title on Tank Abbott, possibly for only 24 hours) before settling on other booked outcomes [d584966s4p0].
Following the withdrawal of the original head writer, replacement bookers chose Chris Benoit to win the title in a revised singles match finish, showing how feuds and title changes were rewritten on short notice [d584966s4p0].
Promotions declare championships vacant for real-life issues such as injury or departure, and vacating has been used both for storyline purposes and to account for unavailable champions [d22220471s0p0].
